newsitem.title: CHINA: Dissidents want China to get tough with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Dissidents want China to get tough with Japan.

text.p: Two of China's most prominent dissidents on Monday demanded Beijing get tough with Tokyo by conducting missile tests near a group of disputed islands in the East China Sea.

"Force can be used against Taiwan, force can be used against students, but force cannot be used against Japan. What is the reason?" Wang Xizhe and Liu Xiaobo said in a joint statement in reference to China's missile tests off Taiwan last March and the army crackdown on unarmed student protesters in June 1989.

The dispute over the uninhabited islands, known as the Diaoyus in Chinese and as the Senkakus in Japanese, flared in September when Japanese rightists moved to buttress Tokyo's claim over them by sailing there and repairing a makeshift aluminium lighthouse.

Anti-Japanese sentiment surged in Hong Kong, a British colony which reverts to Chinese rule in mid-1997, when activist David Chan drowned last week after jumping off a protest ship in defiance of a Japanese blockade of the islands.
The dissidents said China should never renounce the use of force to recover the islands and that Beijing's incompetence had helped to fuel the arrogance of Japanese ultranationalists.

They criticised Beijing for banning anti-Japanese protests and discouraging public interest in state affairs, saying a lack of popular interest in national affairs had created a people who were selfish and insensitive, and ripe for corruption.

"Why is it that when brothers make a noise about breaking up the family, the Chinese Communists are not the least softhearted and use force to push each other?" the dissidents said in apparent reference to China's war games last March aimed at cowing Taiwan into dropping any dreams of independence.

"But when outsiders occupy our territory, the Chinese Communist government can indefinitely shelve the issue and show understanding?" said the statement, a copy of which was made available to Reuters.

Both China and Japan are reluctant to strain their relations and are slightly at a loss over how to deal with the two-month-old wave of nationalist passion that has swept Chinese communities in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau.

Beijing and Taipei, rivals since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949, agree the Diaoyus have been China's for centuries and dispute Tokyo's claim, which dates to 1895 when Japan defeated imperial China in a war and seized the islands.

In a bold move, the two dissidents demanded Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin be indicted, impeached and step down for violating the constitution for saying the People's Liberation Army was under the "absolute leadership" of the party instead of the state.
The dissidents urged the authorities to fulfil a promise in 1945 to give people religious freedom, freedom of the press and speech and to form political parties and stage demonstrations.
They also called for talks between Chinese authorities and Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, saying China had failed to live up to its promise to give Tibet autonomy.
The Tibetan god-king ended a two-week visit to Australia on Monday that left relations between Beijing and Canberra strained because of his meetings with Australian leaders.
The Dalai Lama flew back to India, where he has lived since fleeing his Himalayan homeland after an abortive uprising against Chinese rule in 1959.
